title: Build, Package, and Development Tool Integration
subtopics: Stopping workflows when required steps fail
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Build, Package, and Development Tool Integration and identify at least two relevant syllabus points.
Apply build, package, and development tool integration in a small Bash example and verify the expected output or status.
Identify one edge case or failure mode and state how to test it safely.

content.intro: A build or test pipeline should stop when a required stage fails and preserve logs for diagnosis.
content.why_it_matters: Build, Package, and Development Tool Integration matters because reliable shell automation depends on making this behavior explicit, testing its boundaries, and documenting environment assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson focuses on build, package, and development tool integration. Connect the listed syllabus points to a minimal example, then verify normal behavior, a boundary case, and an expected failure before using the pattern in automation.

items.title: Running build commands
items.text: Define what “Running build commands” means in this lesson, show it with a minimal example, and verify the expected result plus one limitation or edge case.

items.title: Executing test suites
items.text: Make the check repeatable, include a failing case, and record its result; static checks complement but do not replace behavioral tests.

items.title: Capturing build logs
items.text: Separate normal output from diagnostics, include enough non-sensitive context to investigate a failure, and test the resulting output format.

items.title: Stopping workflows when required steps fail
items.text: Define what “Stopping workflows when required steps fail” means in this lesson, show it with a minimal example, and verify the expected result plus one limitation or edge case.

content_blocks.title: How it fits into Bash
content_blocks.text: A build or test pipeline should stop when a required stage fails and preserve logs for diagnosis. Distinguish warnings from failures, declare tool versions, and avoid continuing to a release or deployment after a failed prerequisite.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in a temporary practice file and run it with the locally installed Bash interpreter. The CodeLeaf in-page preview displays reference output only; it does not execute Bash code. Some examples require commands already installed on your machine.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Discard the temporary file or reset the editor to the original snippet. The examples are designed not to modify important data.

content_blocks.title: Watch out
content_blocks.text: Keep data separate from commands, handle timeouts and errors, and use a purpose-built tool for complex structured-data transformations. Do not assume the same command options or newer Bash features exist on every operating system.

content_blocks.title: Check your result
content_blocks.text: Compare the observed output and exit status with the reference behavior. Change one input at a time, include a boundary or invalid input, and note what differs on your target Bash/utility version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety note
content_blocks.text: Use a local test directory, avoid secrets in commands/history/logs, and check the installed interpreter with `bash --version`. This course remains draft until technical examples and assessments receive subject-matter review.

content.task: Build a small local example for “Build, Package, and Development Tool Integration” using synthetic input or a disposable practice directory. Explain what the command should do, check its output and exit status, and test one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use an example aligned with the lesson and preserve arguments, paths, or streams correctly.
Record the observed output and exit status.
Test one boundary case or expected failure.
State the Bash version and any external utility dependency that matters.
hints: Reduce the problem to one command or one small function first.
Use quoting and printf to make argument boundaries visible.
Check exit statuses as well as printed output; use syntax-only validation before testing changes.
content.expected_output: A documented example for “Build, Package, and Development Tool Integration” with the observed output/status, one tested boundary case, and an explicit statement of any version or utility dependency.
troubleshooting: If the snippet uses an external command, check availability with `command -v NAME` and consult that program’s local help.
If behavior differs by operating system or Bash version, record `bash --version` and check the official manual linked below.
For syntax-only validation run `bash -n script.sh`; this parses but does not execute the script.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a successful-looking output means the command succeeded.
common_mistakes.why: Output and exit status are separate signals, and a later command may replace `$?`.
common_mistakes.fix: Capture important statuses immediately and check all relevant pipeline stages.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying example commands straight into a production path.
common_mistakes.why: Real paths, permissions, input names, and external utility versions differ.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable fixture and inspect the planned side effects first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating Bash-specific syntax as portable `sh` syntax.
common_mistakes.why: Arrays, `[[ ... ]]`, process substitution, and some parameter operators are extensions.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the interpreter and test the minimum supported version.

summary: Build, Package, and Development Tool Integration has specific syntax and behavior; verify it rather than relying on guesswork.
Preserve argument boundaries and keep shell commands separate from untrusted data.
Test successful, boundary, and failure cases in a safe environment.
